mag4ot: This week the world fills up with things. To talk about them you need to know whether they are masculine or feminine, how the plural is formed, which article to use, and how to say that something **is** (or **isn't**) in a place. And since you'll come across many new words, you also learn to ask what they mean.
gn59kx: In Spanish **all nouns have gender**: masculine or feminine. For things, gender has nothing to do with sex: _la mesa_ isn't «feminine» in any sense; it's simply grammar.
8ytdlo: Often the ending of the word helps you. Words in **-o** are normally masculine: _el libro, el cuaderno, el bolígrafo_. Words in **-a** are normally feminine: _la mesa, la silla, la mochila_. Words in **-ción**, **-sión**, and **-dad** are feminine: _la habitación, la televisión, la ciudad_.
sb4c76: Words in **-e** or in another consonant can be either gender: _el reloj, el lápiz, la llave, la luz, el cine, la calle_. With these words, the only sure strategy is to **learn the word with its article**.
1t6a3i5: There are some very common exceptions: **el día, el mapa, el problema, el sofá** (masculine in -a) and **la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio** (feminine in -o; _foto_ and _moto_ are short forms of _fotografía_ and _motocicleta_).
1n1exv8: For people, many words change like last week's nationalities: _el chico, la chica_. Others are the same and only the article changes: **el estudiante, la estudiante**.
1ow5lp0: _Mapa_ ends in -a, but it's masculine. It's a very common exception.
xw48ir: The rule is very regular. If the word ends in a **vowel**, add **-s**: _libro → libros_, _llave → llaves_, _silla → sillas_.
1r9x6e7: If it ends in a **consonant**, add **-es**: _reloj → relojes_, _papel → papeles_, _ciudad → ciudades_.
r7jza5: If it ends in **-z**, the z changes to **c** and you add -es: _lápiz → lápices_, _luz → luces_. In Spanish _ze_ or _zi_ is almost never written.
4hpp2o: Watch the accent mark: _habitación_ → **habitaciones** (no accent mark), just like _inglés → ingleses_ last week. When you add a syllable, the word no longer needs the accent mark. And the other way around: _joven → jóvenes_ needs a new accent mark.
rt37c9: For a mixed group of people the masculine plural is used, as with nationalities: _el chico + la chica = los chicos_.
zmg63j: In the plural, _habitaciones_ no longer has an accent mark.
1nux95x: Articles agree with the noun in gender and number. There are two families. The **definite** ones: **el, la, los, las**. The **indefinite** ones: **un, una, unos, unas**.
15t8adw: **Un / una** introduce something **new** to the listener, or any one of a group: En la mesa hay **un** libro. **El / la** talk about something **known**, already mentioned, or unique in the situation: **El** libro es de Nicolás. We also use _el / la_ for something unique: **la** puerta de la habitación (the room has one door).
1k32to: _Unos / unas_ means «some, an imprecise amount»: _unas llaves_, _unos cuadernos_. With numbers no indefinite article is used: _dos sillas_, not _unas dos sillas_ (that means «about two»).
wcsa1n: Another difference from English: to talk about professions or nationalities with _ser_, _un/una_ is not used: **Soy estudiante**, not _Soy una estudiante_.
1mxfhir: With _ser_ + profession or activity, _un/una_ is not used.
n2s3p3: The article agrees in gender and number: masculine plural → **los**.
1meym2g: Hay: saying what there is in a place
19jy36m: **Hay** says that something **exists** or **is present** in a place. It's one single form for singular and plural: _Hay una cama. Hay dos camas._
19ff0el: After _hay_ you use **un / una / unos / unas**, a **number**, or a **plural noun without an article**: _Hay un clóset_, _Hay tres sillas_, _Hay libros en la mesa_. You don't say _hay el / hay la_: the definite article introduces something already known, and _hay_ introduces something new.
l20x6u: To ask: **¿Hay wifi?** **¿Hay una farmacia aquí?** To negate, **no hay**: _No hay televisión_. With _no hay_ the noun often stands alone, without _un/una_: _No hay toallas. No hay mesa._

sxwcc1: In every Spanish word there is **one syllable stronger** than the others: the stressed syllable. In _mesa_ it's **me**; in _reloj_ it's **loj**; in _lámpara_ it's **lám**. The strong syllable is a little longer and higher, but the vowel **doesn't change**: all five vowels sound clear in every syllable.
gzcclf: Changing the strong syllable can change the word: **pa**pa (potato, in Latin America _papa_) / pa**pá** (father); **sá**bana (bed sheet) / sa**ba**na (African landscape).
1c00o8a: The good news: the accent mark tells you where the stress is when the word doesn't follow the general rule. **Rule 1:** if the word ends in a vowel, **-n**, or **-s**, the strong syllable is the second-to-last: _me-sa, li-bro, si-llas, ha-blan_. **Rule 2:** if it ends in another consonant, it's the last: _re-loj, pa-pel, ciu-dad_. If the word doesn't follow these rules, it takes an accent mark: _lá-piz_, _in-glés_, _ha-bi-ta-ción_, _so-fá_. And if the strong syllable is the third-to-last, it always takes an accent mark: _lám-pa-ra, bo-lí-gra-fo, Mé-xi-co_.
1tuldn5: Variation: some words have different stress depending on the country. In Latin America it's _video_ (vi-**de**-o) and in Spain _vídeo_ (**ví**-de-o). In Mexico _chofer_ (cho-**fer**), in Spain _chófer_ (**chó**-fer). The name _Oaxaca_ is pronounced oa-**xa**-ca, and the **x** sounds like **j** (just as in _México_).
1n81p6n: The accent mark is written over the vowel of the strong syllable: á, é, í, ó, ú. One-syllable words normally don't take an accent mark (_mes, pan, luz_). On phone keyboards, hold down the vowel to see the accent mark.
12hh2lz: Three penultimate-stress words: stress on the second-to-last, **me**-sa, **si**-lla, **ca**-ma. The vowel of the weak syllable stays clear.

g911dg: **Có**-mo, es-pa-**ñol**: a phrase you'll use a lot, with two clear stresses.
